title: Prefix Max Maximization via Global Maximum Front-Placement
approach_explanation: To maximize the sum of prefix maximums with at most one swap, the optimal strategy is to place the overall maximum element of the array at the very first position ($a_1$). When the maximum element is at the first position, every prefix from index 1 to $n$ will have this maximum element as its prefix maximum. Thus, the prefix maximum for every single position becomes the global maximum. The maximum possible sum is therefore $n 	imes 	ext{max}(a)$, which can always be achieved by swapping the global maximum with $a_1$ (or doing nothing if it's already at $a_1$).

code_breakdown.explanation: Reads the number of test cases $t$ and enters a while loop to process each test case independently.
Reads the size of the array $n$, handles the edge case where $n=0$ (though constraints say $n 	ext{ geq} 2$), and reads all $n$ integers into a vector.
Iterates through the array to find the maximum element present in the array (`max_ele`).

Computes the maximum possible prefix sum array value by multiplying the global maximum by $n$ (since every prefix max will be equal to this global maximum after the optimal swap) and prints the result.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: For each testcase, we iterate through the array of size $n$ twice: once for reading the elements and once for finding the maximum element. With $t$ test cases, the total time complexity is $O(\sum n)$, which is bounded by $O(t \cdot n)$. Given $t \le 100$ and $n \le 50$, total operations are around $5000$, executing well within the 1.5-second time limit.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: A vector of size $n$ is allocated for storing the array elements per test case, leading to $O(n)$ auxiliary space.

strengths: Extremely concise and optimal $O(n)$ time solution.
Correctly identifies the greedy property that moving the maximum element to the front maximizes all prefix maximums simultaneously.
edge_cases_handled: Handles arrays with already sorted or reverse-sorted elements correctly.
Handles arrays where the maximum element is already at the first index.
best_practices_feedback: Use `std::max_element` from the `<algorithm>` library to find the maximum element more idiomatically.

Prefer `
` over `std::endl` to avoid unnecessary stream flushes and improve I/O performance.

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: Using `std::max_element(a.begin(), a.end())` reduces boilerplate code and improves readability while retaining the exact same optimal asymptotic complexity.
